sentences.text: Fossils of Luperosuchus come from the Chañares Formation in Argentina, where only a single atlas intercentrum—a small bone at the base of the neck—and an incomplete skull have been preserved.
The preserved part of the skull measures 54.5 cm long, implying a total length of about 60 cm, and features a tall, mediolaterally compressed crest on the front of the snout.
Romer noted fused sutures in the skull, indicating the animal was mature, a finding later confirmed by studies showing fully fused bones with well-developed sculpting.
Luperosuchus was one of the largest carnivores and one of the few large animals found in the Chañares Formation.
Its most striking feature is a tall, mediolaterally compressed crest located on the front of its snout.
The holotype specimen PULR 04 was collected by Ruth Romer on January 17, 1965, and Alfred S. Romer published the description of the genus Luperosuchus in 1971.
Diet: Luperosuchus was one of the largest carnivores and one of the few large animals in the Chañares Formation.
Growth: The locality where the fossils were found provides a minimum age of 236.1 +/- 0.6 million years.
Romer originally classified Luperosuchus as a member of the family Rauisuchidae in 1971, and it is classified as a reptile belonging to that same family.
Luperosuchus lived during the latest Ladinian stage of the late Middle Triassic or the earliest Carnian of the Late Triassic, specifically between 241.464 and 237 million years ago.
The early environment was a braided river system with periodic flooding, which later changed to include volcanic deposits like tuff and ash, indicating regional volcanism.
It is debated whether specimen PULR-V 057 belongs to Luperosuchus or represents a distinct taxon, with some researchers suggesting the differences are taxonomic rather than due to age.
